newsitem.title: LATVIA: INTERVIEW-LUKOIL HOPES FOR MORE BALTIC EXPANSION.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-LUKOIL HOPES FOR MORE BALTIC EXPANSION.

text.p: LUKoil Baltija, a subsidiary of Russian oil company LUKoil, said on Monday it plans to increase its share of the Baltic filling station market from the present 17 percent in the next two years.

LUKoil Baltija chief Khaim Kogan also told Reuters in an interview that LUKoil sales in 1996 of oil products in Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia rose 40 percent to 1.074 million tonnes against 367,000 tonnes the previous year.
"In 1996 LUKoil had some 17 percent of the Baltic market, and in 1997 we plan to keep our share in Lithuania and Estonia and expand in Latvia," Kogan added.
LUKoil currently claims around 25 percent of the filling station market in Lithuania and 16 percent in Estonia.
"Latvia currently is somewhere in-between and we plan to build some 10 more stations in two years time," Kogan said.
The number of LUKoil stations in Latvia would then reach 20 from the current 10.
"We have some 23 stations in Lithuania, and some 14 in Estonia," Kogan added.
As well as selling oil products in the Baltic states, LUKoil Baltija also exported some 1.158 million tonnes of crude and oil products in 1996.
The product was exported via Latvia's Ventspils Nafta terminal as well as some diesel fuel through Klaipeda in Lithuania and fuel oil through Tallinn, Kogan said.
Kogan said LUKoil could be more competitive than Western companies, many of which have now invaded the Baltic market.
He said that quality was also not much lower than the petrol of firms like Shell, Neste and Statoil, which is mostly imported from the West.
"World prices this year are such that it is more interesting to sell on the Baltic market than to export it," Kogan said.
Kogan said that Ventspils was still by far its biggest outlet for crude and diesel while Lithuania also offered the chance to process crude in the Mazeikai refinery and then export it via Klaipeda.
Kogan said that the company's future activities would not be influenced by the animosity that exists between Latvia and Russia over the status of Russian-speakers in Latvia.
Kogan said that business rather than Russian-Baltic relations guided LUKoil.
